lesson.title: What Actually Broke the Union: Untangling the Causes of the Civil War
lesson.summary: Slavery sat at the center of every major sectional dispute of the 1850s, and the interlocking crises of Bleeding Kansas, the Dred Scott decision, and the Election of 1860 turned decades of political argument over its expansion into an armed conflict.
lesson.body:
Historians sometimes describe the Civil War's causes as a tangle of economic, cultural, and constitutional disputes between North and South, and all of those disputes were real. The North had industrialized rapidly and built an economy oriented around free wage labor, while the South remained committed to plantation agriculture built on enslaved labor, and the two regions increasingly disagreed over tariffs, federal spending on infrastructure, and how much power the central government should hold relative to the states. But nearly every one of these disputes, when traced back far enough, connected to slavery, either the question of whether it would be allowed to expand into new western territories or the question of what obligations free states owed to a slaveholding South.

The territorial question grew more explosive with each new acquisition of land. The Missouri Compromise of 1820 had drawn a line meant to settle where slavery could and could not spread, but the Mexican-American War added vast new territory that reopened the entire argument, and the Kansas-Nebraska Act of 1854 replaced the old compromise line with the principle of popular sovereignty, letting settlers in each territory vote on slavery for themselves. The result in Kansas was years of violence between pro-slavery and free-state settlers, a preview in miniature of the war to come, and the political fallout gave birth to the Republican Party, built specifically around opposition to slavery's expansion.

The Supreme Court then made the crisis worse rather than better. In its 1857 decision in Dred Scott v. Sandford, the Court ruled not only that Scott, an enslaved man who had lived in free territory, had no standing to sue for his freedom, but also that Congress had no constitutional authority to ban slavery in the territories at all, effectively declaring the old Missouri Compromise line unconstitutional from the start. Chief Justice Roger Taney's opinion went further still, holding that Black Americans, free or enslaved, could not be considered citizens under the Constitution. The ruling delighted Southern slaveholders and horrified much of the North, convincing many Northerners that a Slave Power was working through every branch of the federal government to force slavery into every corner of the country.

By the time of the Election of 1860, the two national parties that had once bridged the sectional divide had broken apart, and a Republican Party built entirely around Northern opposition to slavery's expansion won the presidency without needing a single Southern electoral vote. To Southern political leaders, this proved that the federal government itself, not just individual policies, had permanently slipped out of their control. Secession followed within weeks, and once the Confederacy fired on Fort Sumter in April 1861, whatever remained of the debate over compromise gave way to a war that would not end until slavery itself was destroyed.
